opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to get into it is to start with what a singularity *isn't*. The classical picture people carry around, often without realizing it, comes from regular statistical models: you have a parameter space, and near the true parameter the loss looks like a nice quadratic bowl. Every direction you move away from the optimum costs you something, and the Hessian is full rank. In that world, the number of parameters is basically the measure of complexity, and things like the BIC tell you how to trade off fit against model size.

Neural networks just aren't like that. The map from parameters to functions is massively non-injective: lots of different weight settings compute exactly the same function. Permutation symmetries, rescaling symmetries in ReLU networks, dead neurons, units whose outgoing weights are zero so their incoming weights don't matter. So the set of parameters that achieve minimal loss isn't a point; it's some complicated geometric object, an analytic variety, and that object has singular points where it crosses itself, has cusps, or changes dimension. Near those points the loss is degenerate. It's flat in some directions to all orders, or it goes up like a quartic instead of a quadratic.

What Sumio Watanabe showed, and this is the foundation of singular learning theory, is that the geometry of those singularities governs learning and generalization. The key invariant is the real log canonical threshold, which we call the learning coefficient. Roughly, it measures the *effective* dimensionality of the solution near a point. If you count how much parameter-space volume sits at loss below epsilon as epsilon goes to zero, that volume scales like epsilon to the power of the learning coefficient. More singular points have more volume nearby, a smaller learning coefficient, and they're effectively simpler.

So my one-sentence answer is that singularities represent simplicity, or at least a geometric form of it. A singular point is a solution where the network has degrees of freedom it isn't really using, where there are many ways to perturb the parameters without changing the computation. The Bayesian posterior, and we think to a meaningful extent SGD, is drawn toward those regions, because that's where the volume is. That's a large part of why these massively overparameterized models don't overfit the way the classical theory says they should: the number of parameters is the wrong measure, and the learning coefficient is the right one.

The part I find most exciting, and what's motivated a lot of our work at Timaeus, is that it's not just one global number. Different singularities correspond to qualitatively different solutions, different algorithms the network might implement. Over training, the network can move between them, trading a bit of loss for a big change in complexity or the reverse. Those transitions show up as phase transitions, and we can detect them by estimating the local learning coefficient as training proceeds. In small transformers, those changes line up with the model acquiring new structure, like induction heads.

So the singularities aren't a technical nuisance to be smoothed away. They're the structure. If you want to understand what a network has learned and how it got there, the geometry of those degenerate points is, I think, one of the most principled handles we have, and a natural bridge between learning theory and interpretability.

r001.rationale: The response says different singularities can correspond to different qualitative solutions or algorithms, but it does not clearly state that they represent different predictive solutions at a given loss level. It instead describes transitions that may trade off loss and complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of singular learning theory, and I think the way to come at it is to first ask what the loss landscape looks like from the point of view of the parameters. Suppose you've got a network with some parameter vector w, and you have a loss function L(w). The classical picture that everybody has in their head from statistics or from convex optimization is that near a minimum, the loss looks like a bowl. You can approximate it by a quadratic, the Hessian is positive definite, and everything is nice. That's what we'd call a regular model.

The thing that Watanabe pointed out, and which really is the starting point for all of this, is that neural networks are not like that. The set of parameters that achieve the minimum loss is not a single point. It's not even a nice smooth manifold. It's typically some complicated algebraic variety with self-intersections, cusps, places where the dimension changes. And the reason is pretty intuitive once you think about it. If you have two neurons in a layer and they compute the same function, you can swap them, you can redistribute the weights between them, you can set one of them to zero and scale the other one up. All of those operations give you different parameters but the same function, and therefore the same loss. So you get these directions in parameter space along which the loss is flat, and the geometry of how those flat directions intersect each other is where the singularities live.

So the first-order answer to your question is: a singularity is a point where the Hessian is degenerate, where the quadratic approximation fails. But I think that's not really what the singularities represent. What they represent, in my view, is the structure of the function that the network has learned. And the precise way to say that is through a quantity called the local learning coefficient, which Watanabe calls the real log canonical threshold.

The way to think about it is as follows. If you have a regular model with d parameters, then the volume of the region of parameter space where the loss is less than some small epsilon scales like epsilon to the d over two. That's just the bowl. In a singular model, it scales like epsilon to the lambda, where lambda is this learning coefficient, and lambda is generally less than d over two. So lambda is a kind of effective dimension. It's counting how many parameters are actually being used to specify the function, after you account for all of the degeneracy.

And here's the thing that I find really compelling. More singular, in the sense of smaller lambda, corresponds to simpler. A solution where lots of the parameters don't matter, where you have a lot of degeneracy, is one where the function being computed is in some sense low-complexity. So the singularities are encoding something like an Occam's razor. The geometry of the loss landscape near a solution tells you how complex that solution is, in a way that the raw parameter count completely misses.

And then the free energy formula, which is the central result of Watanabe's work, says that the Bayesian posterior concentrates on regions where you trade off low loss against low lambda. So there's a genuine preference built into Bayesian learning for these highly singular, simple solutions. Whether SGD does something analogous is a question that I think is still open, but empirically it seems to be at least in the right neighborhood.

So when I look at a singularity, I'm not really thinking of it as a pathology or a technical obstacle. I think of it as a geometric signature of structure. The network has found a way of computing something that has a lot of internal redundancy, and that redundancy is visible in the loss landscape as a degeneracy. And the interpretability program that we've been pursuing is really about asking whether you can read that structure off, whether you can go from the local geometry to a statement about what the network is doing. I think that's possible, and the early results on things like developmental stages during training suggest that the learning coefficient is tracking something real about the model's internal organization as it evolves.

r001.rationale: The response describes singularities as parameter degeneracies that reveal a learned function’s structure and complexity. It does not interpret different kinds of singularities as different predictive solutions at a given loss level.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful way to understand them is in terms of redundancy in the way a neural network represents a function. You have this enormous space of parameters, but different points in that space can describe exactly the same input-output behavior.

For example, suppose two hidden units compute the same feature. You can redistribute their outgoing weights while keeping their sum fixed, and the function computed by the network doesn’t change. But if those units compute different features, that freedom generally disappears. So the geometry of the parameters representing a particular function can change from place to place. That’s where singularities enter.

It’s worth distinguishing that from just saying the loss landscape has a flat direction. The deeper issue is that the relationship between parameters and functions becomes degenerate. Some parameter changes are invisible to the model’s behavior, or only become visible at higher orders.

From the perspective of singular learning theory, this matters because learning doesn’t simply select an isolated minimum and sit there. You have to understand the volume and geometry of the nearby parameters that also perform well. Singularities help determine that geometry, and therefore the effective complexity of a solution. So they’re not merely mathematical defects in the landscape—they’re part of how we describe the fact that a very large network can behave like a much simpler model.

r001.rationale: The response explains singularities through parameter redundancy and changes in the geometry of parameters representing a function. It does not interpret different kinds of singularities as different predictive solutions at a given loss level.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as places where the parameters cease to be a faithful description of what the network is doing. You can change the parameters, sometimes in whole families of directions, without changing the function that the network computes.

Take a simple example: suppose an output weight is zero. Then the parameters of the neuron feeding into that weight can vary without affecting the output. Or you might have two neurons doing the same thing, so you can redistribute their contributions without changing the function. Those redundancies give the space of models a geometry that isn't captured by the usual picture of an isolated minimum with a nice quadratic bowl around it.

There's a technical distinction here: singularities aren't simply points where the loss looks sharp or strange. They're failures of identifiability in the statistical model, and they can produce degenerate curvature in the loss.

What makes that interesting is that different ways of representing a function can have different amounts of nearby parameter space that also perform well. So the geometry around a solution matters, not just the loss at the solution. Singular learning theory gives us a way to quantify that geometry and connect it to statistical complexity and generalization. In that sense, singularities tell us something about the effective simplicity of the computation the network has learned, rather than just how many parameters it has.

r001.rationale: The response describes parameter redundancies and different representations of the same function, but does not interpret different kinds of singularities as different predictive solutions at a given loss level.
